title: C++ Concurrency Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on C++ threads, locking, condition variables, atomics, async/futures, and the data races and deadlocks they cause.

chapters.title: Threads and the Concurrency Mental Model
points: std::thread starts running the callable immediately on construction; arguments are copied or moved into the thread, so use std::ref to pass a reference
A joinable thread must be join()ed or detach()ed before destruction, otherwise std::terminate is called
std::jthread (C++20) joins automatically in its destructor and carries a std::stop_token for cooperative cancellation via request_stop()
A thread object is move-only; hardware_concurrency() gives a hint of the core count, and it may return 0
An exception escaping a thread function calls std::terminate; catch inside the thread or pass it out with std::exception_ptr

chapters.title: Mutexes and Lock Wrappers
points: std::mutex provides lock() and unlock(); never call them by hand, use an RAII wrapper so the unlock happens on every exit path including exceptions
lock_guard is the simplest RAII lock: it locks in the constructor, unlocks in the destructor, and cannot be unlocked early or moved
unique_lock is movable, can defer locking (std::defer_lock), unlock early, and is required by condition_variable::wait
scoped_lock (C++17) locks several mutexes at once with a deadlock-avoidance algorithm: std::scoped_lock lk(m1, m2)
std::recursive_mutex allows the same thread to relock, but it usually hides a design problem; shared_mutex with shared_lock allows many readers and one writer

chapters.title: Condition Variables
points: condition_variable lets a thread sleep until another thread signals that a condition changed; the waiter holds a unique_lock on the mutex that protects the condition
Always wait with a predicate: cv.wait(lk, [&]{ return ready; }); this handles spurious wakeups and lost notifications
wait atomically releases the mutex while sleeping and reacquires it before returning
Change the shared state under the mutex, then call notify_one() or notify_all(); notify_all wakes every waiter, so use it when several threads may proceed
Mistake: waiting without a predicate, or modifying the flag without the mutex, causes lost wakeups and data races

chapters.title: Atomics and Memory Order Basics
points: std::atomic<T> makes single operations on T indivisible with no data race: load, store, exchange, fetch_add, compare_exchange_strong/weak
compare_exchange_weak may fail spuriously, so use it in a retry loop; the strong version fails only when the value really differs
The default memory_order_seq_cst gives one global order of all atomic operations and is the safest choice
memory_order_relaxed guarantees only atomicity with no ordering, which suits plain counters; release on a store paired with acquire on a load publishes earlier writes to the reader
volatile is not atomic and gives no thread safety in C++; atomic ops on a struct need it to be trivially copyable, and is_lock_free() tells whether a lock is used

chapters.title: Async, Futures and Promises
points: std::async(fn, args) returns a std::future<T>; future.get() blocks until the result is ready and rethrows any exception, and can be called only once
The default launch policy may run lazily and deferred; pass std::launch::async to force a new thread, and std::launch::deferred to run on get()
A future returned from async blocks in its destructor until the task finishes, so ignoring the returned future makes the call synchronous
std::promise<T> sets a value or exception with set_value/set_exception, and its get_future() gives the reader side; packaged_task wraps a callable the same way
shared_future allows several threads to call get(); wait_for(duration) returns future_status::ready, timeout or deferred

chapters.title: Data Races, Deadlocks and Cheat Sheet
points: Data race: two threads access the same memory without synchronization and at least one writes; this is undefined behaviour, not just a wrong value
Deadlock needs circular wait: thread A holds m1 and wants m2 while B holds m2 and wants m1; fix with scoped_lock or a fixed global lock order
Never call unknown code or callbacks while holding a lock; keep critical sections short and never hold a lock while blocking on I/O
Detect problems with ThreadSanitizer (-fsanitize=thread); the compile flag is -pthread on GCC and Clang
Cheat sheet: jthread over thread; scoped_lock for locking; wait with a predicate; atomic default seq_cst; async with launch::async; keep the future alive
